name: Wendy Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for anyone. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy, 27, and I lead the viola section of a chamber group. I trained through a master’s in music, teach two afternoons, and record parts for local productions. I love the moment a group finds one pulse; I could lose the invoices and the late train rides.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure does that work feel at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earn a fairly ordinary musician’s income and have about three months of expenses saved. I share a flat with my partner, who works at a bakery; I do not count on that wage to cover my half. There are some other music posts nearby, though none is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chamber group that a tidy booking calendar is fine, but the sound is still ours. The audience hears six people listen to each other, not a stack of schedules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm comfortable for a few months, not forever. If bookings hold, I can keep teaching and recording, but my partner's bakery wages aren't my emergency plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the two teaching afternoons and our monthly community hall concert. This winter I'd test an AI invoice checker on my own bills, review every result, and stop if it misreads a fee; through the first year I'd put the saved admin time into practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly settled in this picture. A quiet season still stings, but three months of savings gives me time to call the next venue instead of taking a bad fee tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your small savings cushion let you do here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cushion means I can decline one underpaid recording day and look for a fair one. It would not pay a year's rent if the chamber group folded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine task would you actually hand to a tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over the first pass of matching invoices to dates, if I can check it before anything is sent. I wouldn't give a program my pupils' recordings just to save ten minutes.

say: I would accept a **booking calendar** while defending the chamber group’s live sound.
I would tell colleagues that **schedules** cannot reproduce six musicians listening together.
think: My **three-month cushion** helps with a quiet season, but cannot replace a year’s rent.
I will not treat my partner’s **bakery wage** as my backup plan.
do: Keep two **teaching afternoons** and monthly hall concerts through the first year.
Test an **AI invoice checker** this winter on my own bills, reviewing every result and stopping if fees are misread.
feel: I feel mostly **settled**, with enough savings to refuse one poor fee.
S0.quote: The audience hears six people listen to each other, not a stack of schedules.
fieldNote: Her **typical pay** and three months of savings give her a modest choice over low-fee work.
She permits **limited AI use** on her own invoices, with checking and no pupil recordings.

steps.text: Keep two teaching afternoons and monthly community hall concerts
Test AI invoice checker on own bills and stop if fees are misread

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that booking and score preparation can be quicker, but a shorter task should not mean a smaller musician's fee. I'd push for shared minimums with the local players' association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small recording commissions could go before concerts do. Those parts pay for my teaching room, and I cannot replace them by simply playing louder on stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd learn the new AI score-checking tool from a colleague, using only my own sample parts until I trust it. In the first year, if recording orders shrink, I'd offer a paid ensemble class at the community hall, provided the hall will rent us a room at a price students can cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the side of my work people never see. I can change a lesson, but I cannot conjure a room or ten paying learners overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the first lost fee show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first missing fee would be a short viola part for a local play, usually enough to cover a month's room hire. I'd mark each lost order so I don't mistake a busy concert week for a healthy income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want common rules, but would you use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd use a proven tool to catch a wrong note in a draft. I'd still ask our association for fair recording terms, because one player cannot set the market alone.

say: I would welcome faster **score checks** without accepting lower musician fees.
I would seek shared **fee minimums** through the local players’ association.
think: Small **recording commissions** may disappear before concerts do.
Those commissions cover my **teaching room**, so the loss would reach my main work.
do: Learn a new **AI score-checking tool** with a colleague, using only my own sample parts until I trust it.
Offer a paid **ensemble class** if recording orders shrink, with hall rent covered by paying learners.
Press for fair **recording terms** with the players’ association in the first year.
feel: I feel **anxious** about hidden recording income and uncertain class demand.
S1.quote: I cannot conjure a room or ten paying learners overnight.
fieldNote: She locates the first **income risk** in recorded parts, which currently help pay for the room where she teaches pupils.
Her **class plan** requires affordable hall space and enough paying learners.

steps.text: Learn new AI score checking with colleague on own samples until trusted
Offer ensemble class if recording orders fall and paying learners cover hall rent
Seek shared recording fees through local players’ association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could wipe out arranging and remote coaching, while human-level playing robots follow around 2031. I'd ask the group to plan for two different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording and lesson-planning fees could go quickly, even while audiences still want six living players. Three months of savings buys me a pause, not a replacement for half my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd list which fees come from live playing and which from recordings. In the first year after 2028, if those recording fees fall, I'd cut the rented teaching-room hours, ask the hall about a paid group class, and apply for an open school music post if one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be frightened of a fast income gap, though I would have a plan. The violinist can wait for robot hands until 2031; my recording client can stop calling in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your teaching before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Parents might still pay for a child to play alongside me, but an app could write practice plans in seconds. I would ask each family what part of the lesson they value before changing the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the savings to keep making music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use at most one month's savings to bridge the first cancellations while I seek school work. I won't empty the whole cushion to rent a room that has no pupils.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from capable robots around 2031.
I would ask the chamber group to plan for **separate dates**.
think: Recording and lesson-planning fees could take a **fast hit**.
Three months of savings cannot replace **half my income** for long.
do: List **fee sources** now; cap bridging losses at one month’s savings while seeking school work.
Reduce **teaching-room hours** if recording fees fall after 2028.
Apply for an open **school music post** if the income drops and a vacancy exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a quick income gap, though I have a plan.
S2.quote: Three months of savings buys me a pause, not a replacement for half my income.
fieldNote: Her **high thinking exposure** reaches recording and planning before robot players arrive.
She caps **bridge spending** at one month and keeps school applications conditional on a vacancy.

steps.text: Reduce rented teaching-room hours if recording fees fall after 2028
Ask community hall about paid group class if recording fees fall
Apply for open school music post if income drops and vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association that five years is enough time to put consent and minimum fees in every recording contract. The thinking work changes around 2031; robot players are a later issue around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can move toward group teaching without promising the classes will fill. A longer warning also lets me audition for one of the nearby school posts while I still have steady concert work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd pilot an eight-week viola circle at the hall if the room cost fits paid registrations. Before 2031 I'd ask the association to draft a recording clause; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd keep the circle only if fees cover the room and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but there is room for a careful test. I still know that a five-year forecast doesn't pay this month's teaching-room rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could five years change in your teaching income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If eight pupils pay, the circle could replace one private teaching afternoon without asking my partner to cover it. If only three sign up, I'd keep the private lessons and return the hall booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your musicians’ association to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for permission before recordings are used to train systems and a clear reuse fee. A recording contract without consent and a reuse fee leaves a musician bargaining after the sound has already gone.

say: I would seek **recording consent** and minimum fees before 2031.
I would remind players that capable **robots** follow around 2034.
think: A paid **viola circle** could work, but registration may be too low.
Nearby **school posts** offer a possible option rather than a guaranteed escape.
do: Pilot an **eight-week circle** if paid registration covers hall rent next spring.
Ask the **association** to draft consent and reuse-fee language before 2031.
Keep the **circle** after 2031 only if fees cover the room and my time.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but able to test the class without betting my rent.
S3.quote: A recording contract without consent and a reuse fee leaves a musician bargaining after the sound has already gone.
fieldNote: Five years supports a **small class trial** with an explicit paid-registration threshold and no promise of a full room.
She wants **consent and reuse fees** before recordings move into AI training.

steps.text: Pilot eight-week viola circle if paid registrations cover hall rent
Ask players’ association for recording consent and reuse-fee clause
Continue circle in first year after 2031 only if fees cover room and time
Keep private lessons and return hall booking if only three pupils sign up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players a decade allows time to build live teaching and clearer recording rights. AGI in 2036 is one date; capable robots around 2039 are another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be running a strong local class by then, or the room might be empty. I'm glad I can test it slowly, but I won't pretend a master's degree guarantees a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my chamber and teaching schedule, and save a share of each recording fee while they still come. Across the decade I'd build the viola circle only when registration covers the hall; in the first year after 2036 I'd continue it if pupils still pay for playing together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm cautiously calm about the longer clock, though my income remains seasonal. I can make a series of small choices without putting the whole flat at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use a decade without betting the flat on a forecast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the decade to grow the savings from three months toward six, if the paid work allows it. That cushion would give me a choice if the chamber contract changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that I plan to keep our rent split and show the class numbers each term. I won't ask a bakery shift to underwrite my musical experiment.

say: I would tell younger players to build **live teaching** and secure recording rights.
I would keep **2036 AGI** separate from robots arriving around 2039.
think: A local **class** may grow, but a master’s degree does not guarantee retirement income.
My **seasonal pay** still depends on bookings before any future AI date.
do: Keep **chamber work** and teaching this year.
Save part of each **recording fee** while commissions continue.
Grow the **viola circle** only when registrations cover hall costs.
feel: I feel cautiously **calm** because the decade permits small, affordable tests.
S4.quote: I won't ask a bakery shift to underwrite my musical experiment.
fieldNote: Her ten-year plan grows the **savings cushion** only as paid work permits.
She keeps the **rent split** with her partner and makes class growth conditional on registrations.

steps.text: Keep chamber work and two teaching afternoons this year
Save part of each recording fee while commissions continue
Grow circle when registrations cover hall; continue after 2036 only while pupils pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording and planning fees could vanish before I can replace them. A short paid bridge for teaching space and enforceable recording consent would let me test the hall class without using my whole cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the sound we have already recorded. The viola part I sold for one play should not become an endless free library for somebody else.

headlineQuote: The viola part I sold for one play should not become an endless free library for somebody else.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old violist** with a master’s degree, leading chamber players while teaching and recording parts.
Her **typical musician pay** and three months of savings support careful tests, with some nearby jobs as possible alternatives.
She uses **AI occasionally** on her own work, checking results and keeping pupils’ recordings out of tools.
Fast AGI threatens **recording fees** first; with more time, she tests paid group teaching and presses for recording consent.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could erase recording and planning fees before paid group teaching replaces them.
whatWouldHelp: A short **teaching-space bridge** would help her test a class without draining savings.
Enforceable **recording consent** would protect parts sold for limited uses.
